newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: OAU calls for speedy deployment of force for Zaire.
newsitem.headline: OAU calls for speedy deployment of force for Zaire.

text.p: The Organisation of African Unity called on Monday for the speedy deployment of a neutral force with African participation for eastern Zaire but said the United Nations should pay.

The OAU's Committee for Conflict Prevention, Management and Resolution said after a one-day meeting it regretted the U.N. Security Council had not urgently deployed such a force as urged by an African summit on the Zaire crisis last week in Nairobi.
"Nonetheless given the decision by U.N. Security Council to create a multinational force, the OAU considers that African participation in such a force is pivotal," the committee said in a statement.

After Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi lambasted the United Nations for calling on African states to meet the cost of their participation in a force, the committee appealed for the Security Council to clear the way for African involvement.
"To ensure African participation in the proposed force, financial, logistical and material resources should be provided on a very relaible, dependable and sustainable basis," it said.
It said the mandate of the force -- to provide aid and help the return of Rwandan refugees to Rwanda -- should be clear.
The committee called for the convening of an international solution to find a lasting solution to the crisis in the Great Lakes region of central Africa.
Zaire declined an invitation to Monday's meeting.

Underlining the reluctance of countries to become involved, only nine foreign ministers of the 17 member states of the OAU's conflict committee attended the one-day session in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.
Opening the meeting, Meles said the U.N. Security Council's insistence the cost of the force should be the responsibility of those who took part in it risked leading to further delays.

"The U.N. Security Council decision that the cost of the operation of should be borne by the participating countries ... would naturally make it difficult for African countries to take part in this effort," Meles said.
The OAU itself has been criticised for failing to come up with any meaningful response to the disaster in eastern Zaire.
Some 1.2 million Hutu refugees have fled their camps because of fighting between Tutsi rebels and the Zairean army.
The United States denied on Monday it was blocking creation of an international force to aid the refugees, saying it had still seen no coherent plan for assembling one.

Several ideas are on the table, but only France has launched a diplomatic campaign to try to secure international backing and Paris's motives are deeply distrusted by Rwanda, which supports the Tutsi rebellion.
Meles said he also opposed a 20-day period proposed by U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to send troops to the region.

Meles reiterated Ethiopia's commitment to send troops to the proposed force "provided that principles outlined in the statement by the Nairobi summit are adhered to and provided that all the ground rules for the deployment of the neutral force are worked out by the Security Council."
Among the OAU's 54 states only Ethiopia and Mali have so far pledged to send troops.
East African peace mediator Julius Nyerere asked South African President Nelson Mandela on Saturday to contribute to a Zaire peace force but Mandela said he needed more information.
